paragraphs.text: Childhood-onset growth hormone deficiency (CO-GHD) is an endocrine condition associ ated with a broad range of clinical conse quences, with the most important being failure of linear growth. However, CO-GHD can result in health issues in adulthood, and for this reason, clinical management requires par ticular attention during the transition period, which is the physiological passage from ado lescence to young adulthood. This phase is generally thought to occur from the mid-late teens until approximately 6 or 7 years after final height achievement [1]. The increased survival of children with critical clinical con ditions associated with GHD and treated with GHRT has led to particular attention con cerning the importance of a careful evaluation during the transition period.
paragraphs.heading: Information

paragraphs.text: A number of diagnostic and therapeutic challenges exist once the pediatric indication for GHRT ends. Not all children entering transition have persistent GHD, especially in the “idio pathic” CO-GHD category. On the contrary, patients with anatomic pituitary damage repre sent those who more commonly remain defi cient. Diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up of patients with persistent GHD during transition and adulthood are the subject of this chapter.
paragraphs.heading: Information

paragraphs.text: GHD—isolated or associated with other defi cits—may present during childhood (CO-GHD) or adulthood (AO-GHD). Isolated CO-GHD has an estimated prevalence of 1 patient per 4000–10,000 live births and can be due to mul tiple causes [2]. Based on recently published data, the estimated incidence of combined pitu itary hormone deficiency (CPHD) is 1/16,000 [3]. Approximately 6000 new cases of adults with GHD are diagnosed each year in the United States, with an incidence rate of about 2 per 100,000 people/year [4, 5], and with 15–20% of those cases representing pediatric cases tran sitioning to the adult indication.
paragraphs.heading: of CO-GHD?

paragraphs.text: The “transition period” has been arbitrarily defined as the life phase starting in puberty and ending with full adult maturation, 6–7 years after achieving final height (early to mid-twenties) [1, 6]. For other authors, the end of the transition period can be deter mined from sleep chronotype (switch in time of going to bed), which occurs at a mean of 20.9 years for males or 19.5 years for females [7] or from reaching the total body mineral density (BMD) peak (occurring at a mean age of 26.86 years in males and 22.31 in females) [8]. Up to transition, the role of GHRT in GHD patients is primarily to promote linear growth. After the near-adult height is attained, the GHRT is aimed to prevent abnormal body composition, decreased bone mineral density (which in cases of MPHD can be exacerbated by sex steroid deficiency and/or over-treatment with glucocorticoids or levothyroxine), abnor mal serum lipids, and cardiovascular risk and impaired quality of life [6].
paragraphs.heading: Period”?

paragraphs.text: In the past, GHRT in patients with CO-GHD was stopped after achieving final height, defined as a growth velocity <2 cm/ year [9]. During the past two decades, a growing body of evidence concerning the beneficial effects of continuing GHRT in transition and adult patients with persistent GHD (and of starting GHRT in those with AO-GHD) has led to the increasing usage of recombinant human GH (rhGH) in these patients. GHRT has been proven to posi tively affect the attainment and mainte nance of adult body composition, BMD, metabolic profile (including several bio chemical parameters, such as the lipid pro file), and QoL. These nongrowth promoting effects of GH are very important for body homeostasis and require lifelong GH administration in subjects with permanent
paragraphs.heading: Replacement Therapy Throughout Life?

paragraphs.text: GHD. As many subjects with GO-GHD are no longer GH-deficient when retested at the end of linear growth, the correct reassess ment of CO-GHD is crucial for selecting patients who need lifelong GH therapy [10]. Therefore, the re-evaluation of the GH-IGF-1 axis should be performed in adolescents reaching the transition period who had been previously diagnosed with GHD with few exceptions (see below).
paragraphs.heading: Replacement Therapy Throughout Life?

paragraphs.text: The time for informing the patient and his or her family about the possibility of continuing GHRT through adulthood must remain with the pediatrician or pediatric endocrinologist. “Transitioning” the patient to the adult indi cation requires consultation even before the pediatric indication is completed, so that patient and family can come to an informed decision on whether to continue or discon tinue GHRT, referring them—if necessary— to an adult endocrinologist with an expertise on hypopituitarism and GHD. There is no consensus about the ideal time for shifting the
paragraphs.heading: for Caregivers and Patients During the Transition Period?

paragraphs.text: patient from pediatric to adult services. Some authors suggest transitioning the patient around the age of 19, concurrently to other changes in the patient’s life (e.g., the end of high school) [14–16]. This shift is a very cru cial period, and the counseling must be carefully done. Many factors can increase the risk of dropout during transition, including the differences between pediatric and adult treatment modalities. Young children are less able to understand diseases and therapies and they need caregivers, while adults are more involved in decision-making. Therefore, there are differences in interactions between the patients and their guardians that can influence clinical management and eventually affect patients’ compliance [17].
paragraphs.heading: for Caregivers and Patients During the Transition Period?

paragraphs.text: The identification of CO-GHD patients with persistent GHD is mandatory because the majority of these alterations can be prevented or reduced by GHRT in adult age. In most cases, CO-GHD must be confirmed during the transi tion. However, an analysis of the Hypopituitary Control and Complications Study (HypoCCS) showed that many patients did not continue GHRT during transition, and did not undergo retesting, missing an important window of treat ment [18]. Another retrospective study on 112 patients with CO-GHD indicated that 83% of patients stopped GHRT before transitioning from pediatric to adult care (median age at dis continuation was 16.3 years), but the first reevaluation by an adult endocrinologist occurred much later in life (median age at first visit:

paragraphs.heading: 7.2 Aetiology

paragraphs.text: familial, suggesting the presence of underlying genetic disorders. Idiopathic GHD can be inherited in an autosomal recessive, autosomal dominant, or X-linked recessive manner, usu ally due to mutations in the genes encoding GH (GH1) and the GHRH receptor (GHRHR) [2]. Most cases are sporadic and could be related to a combination of environmental and/or developmental risk factors, including viral infections, vascular or degenerative changes, drug exposure, young maternal age, as is the case for septo-optic dysplasia [20].
paragraphs.heading: 7.2 Aetiology

paragraphs.text: In adults, pituitary tumors, craniopharyn gioma, and other nonpituitary tumors in the sellar area (and related treatments) account for most cases of AO-GHD, although in the past 10 years, an increased rate of idiopathic GHD and other noncommon causes of GHD have been reported [21]. TBI and aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage may account for a subset of GHD cases higher than previously suspected [22]. Data show that the proportion

paragraphs.heading: GHD After Childhood?

paragraphs.text: It is important to remember that other replacement therapies must be optimized in patients with MPHD before retesting: underreplaced hypothyroidism, in particular, can lower IGF-1 levels and cause blunted GH responses at dynamic testing [52]. The altered gonadal function can have effects on GH and IGF1 levels. Hypoadrenalism must be appro priately replaced to avoid the risk related to hypoglycemic stress during testing [53].
paragraphs.heading: GHD After Childhood?

paragraphs.text: The evaluation should start with the measure ment of serum IGF-1 concentration. If IGF-1 is ≥50th percentile for age and gender, it effec tively rules out persistent GHD which is the expected outcome in those with idiopathic, isolated GHD. If the IGF-1 level is ≤50th per centile in individuals with a high likelihood of persistent GHD, formal GH testing may not be needed [6].
paragraphs.heading: 7.4.2.1 Basal Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Hartman et al. have suggested that—with appropriate clinical history of pituitary dis ease—if the IGF-1 serum concentration is <84 ng/mL (utilizing the Esoterix IGF-1 assay) or the pituitary damage causes the loss of three or more pituitary hormones, there is a 98% chance the patient is GHD, making
paragraphs.heading: 7.4.2.1 Basal Evaluation

paragraphs.text: provocative GH testing optional [43]. The value of 84 ng/mL corresponds to an IGF-1 approximately 3 standard deviations (SD) below sex- and age-matched controls for patients older than 28 years. The authors highlighted, however, that even lower SD IGF-1 values are required to obtain such a high positive predictive value in younger patients. Finally, they observed that IGF-1 below 2 SD in comparison to sex- and agematched controls predicted GHD in only 83% of cases, which is inadequate to avoid dynamic testing [43]. Maghnie et al. have confirmed these observations, reporting that a sex- and aged-corrected IGF-1 below 2 SD has a sensi tivity of only 62%, with a consistent overlap between controls, transition patients with iso lated GHD, and those with MPHD [54].
paragraphs.heading: 7.4.2.1 Basal Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Therefore, we can conclude that a low (2–3 SD below normal) IGF-1 can have a diagnos tic value per se in cases of very likely persis tent GHD (three or more pituitary hormone deficiencies plus congenital anomalies, organic causes, iatrogenic damage, or genetic muta tions associated with GHD). A very low IGF-1 (3 SD below sex- and age-matched controls) can have a diagnostic significance, as long as other causes of low IGF-1 are excluded, such as hypothyroidism, liver dis ease, renal failure, malnutrition, and therapy with oral estrogens. All other conditions require provocative testing to confirm a per sistent CO-GHD.

paragraphs.heading: ITT

paragraphs.text: Where GHRH is available, the combined arginine + GHRH test is a viable option to evaluate patients during transition. About 1 μg/kg of GHRH is given intravenously at the beginning of the test, and 0.5 g/kg (maximum 30 g) of arginine is infused over 30 min: blood samples for GH should be taken 30, 60, 90, and 120 min after the start of arginine infusion. This test has very high sensitivity and specific ity both in children and adults [57], but it is deeply influenced by body mass index (BMI): the higher the BMI, the lower the GH peak, and therefore BMI-related cutoffs should be used [58]. Moreover, arginine + GHRH test poses some problems in patients with idio pathic CO-GHD and those with neurosecre tory GHD due to hypothalamic disease, which might be observed after cranial irradiation that was performed within 10 years. In these two diagnoses, the pituitary fails much later than the hypothalamus causing a deficiency in hypo thalamic GHRH with an intact or functioning somatotroph cell pool. Supplying GHRH in the test can result in a false-negative response, as it stimulates only the pituitary secretory capacity: the results of arginine + GHRH test ing may be misleading within 10 years of pitu itary irradiation [38, 59]. A cutoff of GH <9 μg/L after arginine + GHRH has been pro posed for adults with childhood cancer and brain irradiation [60, 61].
The current unavailability of GHRH to use in the arginine + GHRH test in some countries (e.g., the United States) makes an

alternative test necessary. A possible alterna tive is the glucagon stimulation test, although the mechanisms of the GH-stimulatory effect of glucagon remain unclear. Glucagon (1 mg) is given intramuscularly (1.5 mg if the patient is 90 kg in weight or heavier). The sampling for GH during the glucagon test is every 30 min for 4 h [62]: the test may cause discom fort (nausea, vomiting, headache, and sweat ing) and late-onset hypoglycemia. The body of literature about glucagon stimulation test is smaller than for ITT and the argi nine + GHRH test: further refinement of this test has uncovered some categories (over weight patients) where different cutoffs are necessary, as has been confirmed with the arginine + GHRH test [58, 63].

Macimorelin is an orally active ghrelinmimetic that binds to the ghrelin GHS-R1a receptor with a similar affinity to ghrelin. It is rapidly absorbed in the gastrointestinal tract and effectively stimulates endogenous GH secretion [64]. Macimorelin (0.5 mg/kg) is administered as a single oral dose and blood samples for GH should be taken after 30, 45, 60, and 90 min. The main advantage of maci morelin is that the drug is orally administered, without the risk of causing hypoglycemia. The most commonly reported side effect was mild dysgeusia which resolved spontaneously. One drug-related serious adverse event was reported in a subject with an asymptomatic QT interval prolongation on the electrocar diogram. Therefore, careful assessment of the patient’s concurrent medications is recom mended, as well as discontinuation of strong CYP3A4 inducers and drugs associated with the risk of prolonged QT [65]. Macimorelin test results are not influenced by BMI values up to 36 kg/m2 [66].

In summary, ITT, glucagon test, arginine + GHRH (where available), and macimorelin are suggested to provide convincing evidence of persistent GHD. The usage of more than one test may be considered in case of border line or nonconcordant results (e.g., discrep ancy between basal IGF-1 and stimulated GH) or when clinical history poses some chal lenges (e.g., recent brain irradiation). Less stringent tests such as levodopa, clonidine, or arginine alone are currently not suggested,
since they have low sensitivity and specificity for GHD diagnosis [67].

The Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guide line underlined the problem of abnormalities of hypothalamic-pituitary functioning and GH deficiency often observed in childhood cancer survivors [68]. GHD is the most com mon endocrine late effect in childhood cancer survivors treated with cranial radiotherapy, with a different prevalence depending on the type of tumor and treatment. It is most fre quent in survivors of suprasellar tumors and after high-dose hypothalamus-pituitary axis radiotherapy. GHD in the cancer population has similar symptoms as in the general popula tion, and in adults, it may be associated with reduced lean body mass and increased fat mass, an adverse lipid profile, increased cardiovascu lar morbidity, impaired bone mineral density, impaired quality of life, and psychosocial problems [69].
paragraphs.heading: 7.4.2.3 Cancer Survivors

paragraphs.text: Testing with ITT and glucagon has been recommended for the diagnosis of GHD in adult survivors of childhood cancer. A sys tematic review on the diagnosis of GHD as a late effect of radiotherapy in survivors of childhood cancer raises the question of how to interpret the GH response after arginine + GHRH in patients with primary hypotha lamic dysfunction [70].
paragraphs.heading: 7.4.2.3 Cancer Survivors

paragraphs.text: Endocrine Society Guidelines recommend against the use of GHRH alone or in combina tion with arginine in childhood cancer survivors to diagnose GHD after hypothalamus-pituitary axis radiation. In fact, when the damage is pri marily hypothalamic, as after radiation therapy, it may give false-negative results [68]. In conclu sion, the ITT is the most accepted reference test to establish the diagnosis of GHD using a cutoff of GH <5–6 μg/L [53]. When the ITT is contra indicated, the glucagon test seems to be the most preferred alternative, using a cutoff of GH <1 or 3 μg/L, depending on BMI [53].

paragraphs.text: Adult-dose GHRT is recommended if GHD is confirmed during the transition period, in order to complete somatic development, obtain full skeletal maturation, and promote increase of lean mass. Retesting for GHD and—if con firmed—starting GHRT should be done as quickly as possible [34, 46]. In adolescents who decline the offer to continue GHRT, monitor ing of GH-dependent endpoints is required. Evidence of subsequent deterioration consti tutes the basis for reassessment of the decision to reinstate GHRT [1].

During childhood, linear growth is the pri mary outcome of GHRT. It is an objective parameter easily assessed by pediatric endo crinologists. During transition and adult hood, other parameters become important: body composition (including BMI and waist circumference), BMD, lipid profile, and QoL. However, if we consider them sepa rately, none of these measurements shows enough sensitivity and specificity to properly assess the clinical response to GHRT, and physicians mainly use IGF-1 as a biochemical marker of response. Nonetheless, whether an increase in IGF-1 levels reflects a positive clin ical response is still a matter of debate.
paragraphs.heading: the Clinical Response to GHRT in Adults?

paragraphs.text: An analysis of the KIMS International Metabolic Database [103] showed that the worse the initial values of some endpoints (QoL, low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol, and waist-hip ratio), the better the response of the same variable. Additionally, a later analysis of the same database highlighted a sexual dimorphism in the clinical response, with greater responses of BMI in males and of QoL in females [104]. In the wake of these observations, Schneider et al. [105] identified lower IGF-1 values, higher total cholesterol levels, higher waist circumference, and worse QoL (using the QoL-AGHDA questionnaire) at baseline evaluation as the best predictors of the clinical response to 2 years of GHRT. These authors suggest that, given a biochemically proven GHD during adulthood, the basal and 6-month evaluation of the aforementioned parameters may aid the clinician in the deci sion of starting or continuing GHRT. Radovick et al. [31] suggest individu alized indications to treat patients with persis tent CO-GHD during transition on the basis of the diagnosis (isolated GHD vs. MPHD) and of the risk of metabolic complications (considering BMD and body composition). These authors suggest confirming treatment in transitioning patients with MPHD if the risk/benefit ratio is favorable, and the patients agree to continue daily injections. On the con
paragraphs.heading: the Clinical Response to GHRT in Adults?

paragraphs.text: trary, in persistent isolated GHD, GHRT is encouraged in those with an abnormal meta bolic profile (low BMD, high fat mass, low lean body mass). Low-risk patients, however, should be followed up carefully to detect early alterations of these parameters or a worsen ing of the QoL and discuss once again the possibility to restart GHRT.
paragraphs.heading: the Clinical Response to GHRT in Adults?

paragraphs.text: GHRT is usually considered safe in adults. However, several potential adverse effects must be taken into consideration before start ing GHRT and during follow-up. A compre hensive review of the possible complications and side effects in pediatric patients on GHRT can be found in Chap. 1.
paragraphs.heading: and Side Effects Possibly Related to GHRT in Adults?

paragraphs.text: GHD patients may be a category with an intrinsic higher mortality risk. First of all, patients with hypopituitarism, including an assumed GHD but substituted for all other deficiencies except GHD, have an excess mor tality [72]. However, hypopituitarism is often due to complex causes and the reason for the excess mortality can be multifactorial includ ing the etiology of hypopituitarism, nonphysi ological glucocorticoid replacement therapies, and tumor treatment and its side effects. For the same reason, the underlying condition causing GHD (many individuals having a his tory of treated brain neoplasms, previous cra nial irradiation, or subarachnoid hemorrhage) can cause an excess of mortality. Hence, it is very difficult to assess whether GHRT can play a role in affecting all-cause or causespecific mortality. The “Safety and Appropriateness of Growth Hormone Treatments in Europe (SAGhE)” is a study involving approximately 25,000 European patients who received GHRT in childhood during the 1980s and 1990s. The aim of the consortium is to assess the long-term safety of GHRT in these patients, comparing their mortality and cancer risk to the general popu
paragraphs.heading: 7.5.3.1 Mortality

paragraphs.text: lation. A preliminary report of the French SAGhE study raised concerns regarding the safety of GHRT in about 6000 patients who received GH for idiopathic isolated GHD, neurosecretory dysfunction, and idiopathic short stature or born short for gestational age [106]. Despite these categories being regarded as “low risk” for mortality when compared to the general population, the French SAGhE study found an increase of 33% in all-cause mortality in this cohort of patients, especially in those who received >50 μg/kg of daily GH. Bone tumors and cerebral hemorrhage were the main causes of mortality, while the overall risk of cancer-related deaths was not increased. However, a report of the SAGhE study from the Netherlands, Belgium, and Sweden and an analysis of the Hypopituitary Control and Complications Study (HypoCCS) did not confirm these findings [18, 107]. Other retrospective observational studies showed that mortality in GHRT is not different from the general population and that in some cases GHRT has improved the detrimental effects of hypopituitarism attributed to GHD [108]. Consequently, the existing evidence does not support an association between GHRT and mortality risk [109].
paragraphs.heading: 7.5.3.1 Mortality

paragraphs.text: GH and IGF-1 exert anabolic and antiapoptotic effects promoting cellular growth and proliferation. Concerns have conse quently been raised regarding the possible role of GHRT in increasing cancer risk and tumor regrowth [110].
paragraphs.heading: Regrowth

paragraphs.text: The Pediatric Endocrine Society has per formed a review of existing literature on this topic, focusing on children treated with GH and on cancer risk during treatment or throughout long-term surveillance after GHRT withholding [111]. The authors con cluded that GHRT is safe in children without intrinsic risk factors for malignancy (chiefly those with idiopathic CO-GHD), and it is not associated with the development of new pri mary cancer. On the other hand, the existing body of evidence cannot exclude a relation ship between increased cancer risk (second
paragraphs.heading: Regrowth

paragraphs.text: neoplasms) in childhood cancer survivors receiving GHRT [109]. These conclusions underline the necessity to discuss this aspect with patients and their caregivers, assess the risk/benefit ratio in each case, plan a longterm follow-up in patients with a history of pediatric malignancy. On the other hand, the risk of primary tumor regrowth in childhood cancer survivors receiving GHRT should not be a concern if the neoplasm has been suc cessfully treated and there are no signs of active malignancy. A recent meta-analysis showed that GHRT during childhood is not related to all-cause mortality and cancer mor tality, but in contrast, GHRT seems to repre sent a trigger for the development of a second neoplasm [112]. Some studies have reported an increased incidence of bone cancer and bladder cancer in patients treated with rhGH and in patients with Hodgkin lymphoma [113, 114].
paragraphs.heading: Regrowth

paragraphs.text: Sklar reported an increased risk of sec ondary neoplasms in childhood cancer survi vors treated with GHRT, especially osteogenic sarcomas in leukaemia and lymphoma survi vors. An increased risk of central nervous sys tem tumors, mostly meningiomas, has also been reported [115].
paragraphs.heading: Regrowth

paragraphs.text: The association could be explained by the evidence that both meningiomas and osteo genic sarcomas express receptors for GH and IGF-1, and modulation of the GH/IGF-1 axis can affect the growth of these tumors in vitro and in vivo [116].
paragraphs.heading: Regrowth

paragraphs.text: A separate report from the SAGhE study on meningiomas showed that this association is probably due to cranial radiotherapy in childhood cancer survivors and that the role of GH treatment is more uncertain [117].
paragraphs.heading: Regrowth

paragraphs.text: In conclusion, based on the currently available evidence, GHRT seems safe for can cer survivors and it is not associated with an increased risk of primary tumor recurrence. However, this group of patients needs careful monitoring due to the possible increased risk of other tumors [53].
paragraphs.heading: Regrowth

paragraphs.text: There is no consensus regarding the opti mal timing between anti-cancer treatment completion and the start of GHRT, and this should be decided on an individual basis.
paragraphs.heading: Regrowth

paragraphs.text: Evidence regarding cancer risk in adults receiving GHRT is less robust, but publica tions suggest that there is no effect of GHRT on the risk of new primary neoplasms [109]. Data about recurrence of primary cancers and the development of second neoplasms in adult cancer survivors are inconclusive. A recent joint meeting of the European Society of Paediatric Endocrinology, the GH Research Society, and the Pediatric Endocrine Society “did not support cancer surveillance beyond local standard practice in patients (children and adults) currently treated with GH nor in those previously treated with GH (including those with a previous malig nancy)” [109].
paragraphs.heading: Regrowth

paragraphs.text: GHRT can exert complex influences on insu lin sensitivity. On one hand, GH is an insulin counter-regulatory hormone promoting glu coneogenesis in the liver and reducing glucose uptake by hepatocytes. On the other hand, GHD is associated with altered body compo sition (unfavorable lean mass/fat mass ratio) that can lead to insulin resistance and predis pose to impairment of glucose metabolism. A study performed in more than 23,000 children treated with GHRT reported a six-fold increase in the incidence of type 2 diabetes compared to two other age-matched cohorts of untreated children [118]. In addition, data from the Pfizer International Growth Database (KIGS) indicate that GH therapy in children may be associated with an increased incidence of type 2 diabetes mellitus. Diabetes mellitus is not an absolute contraindication to GHRT. However, if the patient has diabetes and GH therapy is started, glycemic control may worsen before it becomes better because of the positive effect on body composition [14]. Likewise, adults predisposed to diabetes (e.g., positive family history, personal history of gestational diabetes, metabolic syndrome) may experience a worsening of blood glucose control [89]. This suggests the importance of enhancing surveillance of individuals at risk for developing diabetes mellitus after the start of GHD. Finally, it is advisable to start GHRT
paragraphs.heading: and Diabetes Mellitus

paragraphs.text: with lower doses in these categories of patients.
paragraphs.heading: and Diabetes Mellitus

paragraphs.text: 122 Patients who received brain radiotherapy are chiefly at risk, as pituitary insufficiency may occur several years after the insult and GHRT might unmask central hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency during long-term follow-up.
paragraphs.heading: 7.5.3.4 Adrenal and Thyroid Function

paragraphs.text: Adverse events reported in adults on GHRT include arthralgia, fluid retention (peripheral edema), paresthesias (especially carpal tunnel syndrome), and reduced concentration [123]. These side effects are dose-dependent and are generally transient. Starting treatment with low doses of GH, gradually titrated upwards, reduces the incidence of these side effects. Benign intracranial hypertension (pseudotu mor cerebri) has been reported as a side effect of GHRT in children [124]. Lower doses of rhGH are recommended in obese patients because they are more susceptible to GHRT side effects.
paragraphs.heading: 7.5.3.5 Other Possible Side Effects

paragraphs.text: Before reinstating GHRT during transition and adulthood, it may be important to con sider the contraindications to GHRT that might exist or have developed since stopping GH therapy. The first and most important would be the development of an active malig nancy. This should be obvious by the history, but the clinician should be aware of this pos sibility. Some patients may have had a central nervous system tumor that was irradiated in childhood. This should be re-examined by an appropriate MRI image of the brain. The tumor may have recurred, or more likely, a new tumor may have developed because of irradiation to the area. Developing a second
paragraphs.heading: for Continuing GHRT?

paragraphs.text: central nervous system tumor is a known risk after cranial irradiation.
paragraphs.heading: for Continuing GHRT?

paragraphs.text: Another contraindication to GHRT is the presence of active proliferative or severe no proliferative diabetic retinopathy, given the proven effects of the GH/IGF-1 axis on the retina in patients with diabetes [125].
paragraphs.heading: for Continuing GHRT?

paragraphs.text: Pregnancy is not an absolute contraindica tion to GH therapy [126]. The placenta pro duces chorionic somatomammotropin during the third trimester (or even earlier) and, there fore, GH is not necessary during the last 3 months of pregnancy [109]. paragraphs.text: A 20-year-old man is sent to you by a neurosur geon for evaluation of his endocrine status. He had normal growth and development but has recently been found to have a craniopharyngi oma identified because of the development of visual field abnormalities. He underwent surgery to remove the tumor. Subsequent to the surgery, he was found to have hypopituitarism. After a year of replacement therapy with testosterone, thyroid hormone, and hydrocortisone, and a stable MRI image of the sellar area, he returns for follow-up care. On physical exam, he weighed 148 kg and was 170 cm tall. His IGF-1 concen tration was undetectable, and he has no GH
paragraphs.heading: IGF-1 (NL

paragraphs.text: response to arginine stimulation testing (all GH concentrations <0.1 ng/mL). His fasting insulin was 48 IU/mL and simultaneous glucose was 115 mg/dL. Because of concerns about his glu cose status, GH therapy was started cautiously. He was started on 0.3 mg s.c. daily. Immediately, he began to have polyuria and polydipsia. This progressed to moderate ketoacidosis over a 1-week period. Because of this rather dramatic and sudden appearance of type 2 diabetes, he did not want to restart GH therapy for fear of going into ketoacidosis again. Very shortly thereafter, he required oral hypoglycemic agents to control his blood glucose. This case repre sents the extreme aggravation of diabetes after beginning GH therapy or exposing latent diabe tes after starting GH therapy. Physicians should be aware of this category of patient when begin ning GH therapy, and in this category, we begin with a small dose of 0.1 mg/day to avoid aggra vation of his insulin resistance.

paragraphs.heading: 7.7 Summary

paragraphs.text: The treatment of adults who have been GHD as children is an emerging clinical science. Until quite recently, the main target of GHRT in patients with CO-GHD was the attainment of full linear growth, and the treatment was stopped as soon as near-adult height was achieved. However, during the last 20 years, the literature has questioned this practice, as the discontinuation of the replacement therapy during adulthood in those with a persistent GHD can cause detrimental effects on body composition, bone health, cardiovascular sys tem, and QoL. As for other chronic conditions, the correct management of persistent GHD during the delicate phase of transition is cru cial. Patients and their families should receive adequate support and information when trans ferred from pediatric to adult endocrine ser vices. The first and foremost important rule is to confirm that the patient is persistently defi cient, especially in patients who carry the diag nosis of idiopathic isolated GHD. A number of issues surround therapy including dosing and monitoring. As time passes, there will be more young adult patients seeking therapy for their GH deficiency. These situations include the trend for pediatricians to suggest continu ing GH after the pediatric indication and adult endocrinologists who are familiar with the care of this group of patients and the patients them selves seeking a solution to their symptoms.

Untreated GHD can therefore have a negative impact on individuals through out their life span. Issues related to lin ear growth are obviously more important in the pediatric population, whereas body composition, bone metab olism, and quality of life (QoL) gradu ally become more important in adults. 5 GHD can occur in pediatric patients (childhood-onset GHD, CO-GHD) or in adults (adult-onset GHD, AO- GHD). Isolated idiopathic GHD is the most common cause of CO-GHD, and most patients revert to a normal GH secretion during transition and young adulthood. AO-GHD is mostly due to secondary damage of the hypothalamicpituitary area and is commonly associ ated with an additional deficit: multiple pituitary hormone deficiencies (MPHD). About 15–20% of AO-GHD cases derive from a CO-GHD persisting during transition and adulthood. 5 After children on GH replacement ther apy (GHRT) achieve adult height, GH should be stopped, and they should be retested to confirm a persistent GHD. Serum IGF-1 measurement can be sufficient to confirm GHD in the minority of patients who are highly likely to remain deficient. All other patients require GH provocative testing. 5 Patients with persistent CO-GHD during transition and adulthood should be treated to attain full body and bone matu ration and to improve their QoL and some cardiovascular risk factors (chiefly the lipid profile). GHRT is generally safe, but GH dosing has to be individualized according to the patient’s characteristics. ### 7.1 Introduction and Background ### Information Childhood-onset growth hormone deficiency (CO-GHD) is an endocrine condition associ ated with a broad range of clinical conse quences, with the most important being failure of linear growth. However, CO-GHD can result in health issues in adulthood, and for this reason, clinical management requires par ticular attention during the transition period, which is the physiological passage from ado lescence to young adulthood. This phase is generally thought to occur from the mid-late teens until approximately 6 or 7 years after final height achievement [1]. The increased survival of children with critical clinical con ditions associated with GHD and treated with GHRT has led to particular attention con cerning the importance of a careful evaluation during the transition period. A number of diagnostic and therapeutic challenges exist once the pediatric indication for GHRT ends. Not all children entering transition have persistent GHD, especially in the “idio pathic” CO-GHD category. On the contrary, patients with anatomic pituitary damage repre sent those who more commonly remain defi cient. Diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up of patients with persistent GHD during transition and adulthood are the subject of this chapter. ### 7.1.1 What Is the Frequency ### of CO-GHD? GHD—isolated or associated with other defi cits—may present during childhood (CO-GHD) or adulthood (AO-GHD). Isolated CO-GHD has an estimated prevalence of 1 patient per 4000–10,000 live births and can be due to mul tiple causes [2]. Based on recently published data, the estimated incidence of combined pitu itary hormone deficiency (CPHD) is 1/16,000 [3]. Approximately 6000 new cases of adults with GHD are diagnosed each year in the United States, with an incidence rate of about 2 per 100,000 people/year [4, 5], and with 15–20% of those cases representing pediatric cases tran sitioning to the adult indication. ## PDF page 192 | printed page 176 ### 7.1.2 What Is the “Transition ### Period”? The “transition period” has been arbitrarily defined as the life phase starting in puberty and ending with full adult maturation, 6–7 years after achieving final height (early to mid-twenties) [1, 6]. For other authors, the end of the transition period can be deter mined from sleep chronotype (switch in time of going to bed), which occurs at a mean of 20.9 years for males or 19.5 years for females [7] or from reaching the total body mineral density (BMD) peak (occurring at a mean age of 26.86 years in males and 22.31 in females) [8]. Up to transition, the role of GHRT in GHD patients is primarily to promote linear growth. After the near-adult height is attained, the GHRT is aimed to prevent abnormal body composition, decreased bone mineral density (which in cases of MPHD can be exacerbated by sex steroid deficiency and/or over-treatment with glucocorticoids or levothyroxine), abnor mal serum lipids, and cardiovascular risk and impaired quality of life [6]. ### 7 ### 7.1.3 What Are the Aims of GH ### Replacement Therapy Throughout Life? In the past, GHRT in patients with CO-GHD was stopped after achieving final height, defined as a growth velocity <2 cm/ year [9]. During the past two decades, a growing body of evidence concerning the beneficial effects of continuing GHRT in transition and adult patients with persistent GHD (and of starting GHRT in those with AO-GHD) has led to the increasing usage of recombinant human GH (rhGH) in these patients. GHRT has been proven to posi tively affect the attainment and mainte nance of adult body composition, BMD, metabolic profile (including several bio chemical parameters, such as the lipid pro file), and QoL. These nongrowth promoting effects of GH are very important for body homeostasis and require lifelong GH administration in subjects with permanent GHD. As many subjects with GO-GHD are no longer GH-deficient when retested at the end of linear growth, the correct reassess ment of CO-GHD is crucial for selecting patients who need lifelong GH therapy [10]. The recom mended “wash-out” time before retesting is a minimum of 1 month [1] and should not exceed 3–6 months [31]. It is important to remember that other replacement therapies must be optimized in patients with MPHD before retesting: underreplaced hypothyroidism, in particular, can lower IGF-1 levels and cause blunted GH responses at dynamic testing [52]. If IGF-1 is ≥50th percentile for age and gender, it effec tively rules out persistent GHD which is the expected outcome in those with idiopathic, isolated GHD. If the IGF-1 level is ≤50th per centile in individuals with a high likelihood of persistent GHD, formal GH testing may not be needed [6]. Hartman et al. have suggested that—with appropriate clinical history of pituitary dis ease—if the IGF-1 serum concentration is <84 ng/mL (utilizing the Esoterix IGF-1 assay) or the pituitary damage causes the loss of three or more pituitary hormones, there is a 98% chance the patient is GHD, making provocative GH testing optional [43]. The value of 84 ng/mL corresponds to an IGF-1 approximately 3 standard deviations (SD) below sex- and age-matched controls for patients older than 28 years. The authors highlighted, however, that even lower SD IGF-1 values are required to obtain such a high positive predictive value in younger patients. Finally, they observed that IGF-1 below 2 SD in comparison to sex- and agematched controls predicted GHD in only 83% of cases, which is inadequate to avoid dynamic testing [43]. Maghnie et al. have confirmed these observations, reporting that a sex- and aged-corrected IGF-1 below 2 SD has a sensi tivity of only 62%, with a consistent overlap between controls, transition patients with iso lated GHD, and those with MPHD [54]. During childhood, linear growth is the pri mary outcome of GHRT. It is an objective parameter easily assessed by pediatric endo crinologists. During transition and adult hood, other parameters become important: body composition (including BMI and waist circumference), BMD, lipid profile, and QoL. However, if we consider them sepa rately, none of these measurements shows enough sensitivity and specificity to properly assess the clinical response to GHRT, and physicians mainly use IGF-1 as a biochemical marker of response. Nonetheless, whether an increase in IGF-1 levels reflects a positive clin ical response is still a matter of debate. An analysis of the KIMS International Metabolic Database [103] showed that the worse the initial values of some endpoints (QoL, low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol, and waist-hip ratio), the better the response of the same variable. Additionally, a later analysis of the same database highlighted a sexual dimorphism in the clinical response, with greater responses of BMI in males and of QoL in females [104]. In the wake of these observations, Schneider et al. [105] identified lower IGF-1 values, higher total cholesterol levels, higher waist circumference, and worse QoL (using the QoL-AGHDA questionnaire) at baseline evaluation as the best predictors of the clinical response to 2 years of GHRT. These authors suggest that, given a biochemically proven GHD during adulthood, the basal and 6-month evaluation of the aforementioned parameters may aid the clinician in the deci sion of starting or continuing GHRT. Radovick et al. [31] suggest individu alized indications to treat patients with persis tent CO-GHD during transition on the basis of the diagnosis (isolated GHD vs. MPHD) and of the risk of metabolic complications (considering BMD and body composition). These authors suggest confirming treatment in transitioning patients with MPHD if the risk/benefit ratio is favorable, and the patients agree to continue daily injections. On the con trary, in persistent isolated GHD, GHRT is encouraged in those with an abnormal meta bolic profile (low BMD, high fat mass, low lean body mass). Low-risk patients, however, should be followed up carefully to detect early alterations of these parameters or a worsen ing of the QoL and discuss once again the possibility to restart GHRT. ### 7.5.3 Are There Complications ### and Side Effects Possibly Related to GHRT in Adults? GHRT is usually considered safe in adults. However, several potential adverse effects must be taken into consideration before start ing GHRT and during follow-up. A compre hensive review of the possible complications and side effects in pediatric patients on GHRT can be found in Chap. 1. ### 7.5.3.1 Mortality GHD patients may be a category with an intrinsic higher mortality risk. First of all, patients with hypopituitarism, including an assumed GHD but substituted for all other deficiencies except GHD, have an excess mor tality [72]. However, hypopituitarism is often due to complex causes and the reason for the excess mortality can be multifactorial includ ing the etiology of hypopituitarism, nonphysi ological glucocorticoid replacement therapies, and tumor treatment and its side effects. For the same reason, the underlying condition causing GHD (many individuals having a his tory of treated brain neoplasms, previous cra nial irradiation, or subarachnoid hemorrhage) can cause an excess of mortality. Hence, it is very difficult to assess whether GHRT can play a role in affecting all-cause or causespecific mortality. The “Safety and Appropriateness of Growth Hormone Treatments in Europe (SAGhE)” is a study involving approximately 25,000 European patients who received GHRT in childhood during the 1980s and 1990s. The aim of the consortium is to assess the long-term safety of GHRT in these patients, comparing their mortality and cancer risk to the general popu ## PDF page 210 | printed page 194 lation. A preliminary report of the French SAGhE study raised concerns regarding the safety of GHRT in about 6000 patients who received GH for idiopathic isolated GHD, neurosecretory dysfunction, and idiopathic short stature or born short for gestational age [106]. Despite these categories being regarded as “low risk” for mortality when compared to the general population, the French SAGhE study found an increase of 33% in all-cause mortality in this cohort of patients, especially in those who received >50 μg/kg of daily GH. Bone tumors and cerebral hemorrhage were the main causes of mortality, while the overall risk of cancer-related deaths was not increased. However, a report of the SAGhE study from the Netherlands, Belgium, and Sweden and an analysis of the Hypopituitary Control and Complications Study (HypoCCS) did not confirm these findings [18, 107]. Other retrospective observational studies showed that mortality in GHRT is not different from the general population and that in some cases GHRT has improved the detrimental effects of hypopituitarism attributed to GHD [108]. Consequently, the existing evidence does not support an association between GHRT and mortality risk [109]. ### 7 ### 7.5.3.2 Cancer Risk and Tumor ### Regrowth GH and IGF-1 exert anabolic and antiapoptotic effects promoting cellular growth and proliferation. Concerns have conse quently been raised regarding the possible role of GHRT in increasing cancer risk and tumor regrowth [110]. The Pediatric Endocrine Society has per formed a review of existing literature on this topic, focusing on children treated with GH and on cancer risk during treatment or throughout long-term surveillance after GHRT withholding [111]. The authors con cluded that GHRT is safe in children without intrinsic risk factors for malignancy (chiefly those with idiopathic CO-GHD), and it is not associated with the development of new pri mary cancer. On the other hand, the existing body of evidence cannot exclude a relation ship between increased cancer risk (second neoplasms) in childhood cancer survivors receiving GHRT [109]. These conclusions underline the necessity to discuss this aspect with patients and their caregivers, assess the risk/benefit ratio in each case, plan a longterm follow-up in patients with a history of pediatric malignancy. On the other hand, the risk of primary tumor regrowth in childhood cancer survivors receiving GHRT should not be a concern if the neoplasm has been suc cessfully treated and there are no signs of active malignancy. A recent meta-analysis showed that GHRT during childhood is not related to all-cause mortality and cancer mor tality, but in contrast, GHRT seems to repre sent a trigger for the development of a second neoplasm [112]. Some studies have reported an increased incidence of bone cancer and bladder cancer in patients treated with rhGH and in patients with Hodgkin lymphoma [113, 114]. Sklar reported an increased risk of sec ondary neoplasms in childhood cancer survi vors treated with GHRT, especially osteogenic sarcomas in leukaemia and lymphoma survi vors. An increased risk of central nervous sys tem tumors, mostly meningiomas, has also been reported [115]. The association could be explained by the evidence that both meningiomas and osteo genic sarcomas express receptors for GH and IGF-1, and modulation of the GH/IGF-1 axis can affect the growth of these tumors in vitro and in vivo [116]. A separate report from the SAGhE study on meningiomas showed that this association is probably due to cranial radiotherapy in childhood cancer survivors and that the role of GH treatment is more uncertain [117]. In conclusion, based on the currently available evidence, GHRT seems safe for can cer survivors and it is not associated with an increased risk of primary tumor recurrence. However, this group of patients needs careful monitoring due to the possible increased risk of other tumors [53]. There is no consensus regarding the opti mal timing between anti-cancer treatment completion and the start of GHRT, and this should be decided on an individual basis. ## PDF page 211 | printed page 195 Evidence regarding cancer risk in adults receiving GHRT is less robust, but publica tions suggest that there is no effect of GHRT on the risk of new primary neoplasms [109]. Data about recurrence of primary cancers and the development of second neoplasms in adult cancer survivors are inconclusive. A recent joint meeting of the European Society of Paediatric Endocrinology, the GH Research Society, and the Pediatric Endocrine Society “did not support cancer surveillance beyond local standard practice in patients (children and adults) currently treated with GH nor in those previously treated with GH (including those with a previous malig nancy)” [109]. ### 7.5.3.3 Glucose Metabolism ### and Diabetes Mellitus GHRT can exert complex influences on insu lin sensitivity. On one hand, GH is an insulin counter-regulatory hormone promoting glu coneogenesis in the liver and reducing glucose uptake by hepatocytes. On the other hand, GHD is associated with altered body compo sition (unfavorable lean mass/fat mass ratio) that can lead to insulin resistance and predis pose to impairment of glucose metabolism. A study performed in more than 23,000 children treated with GHRT reported a six-fold increase in the incidence of type 2 diabetes compared to two other age-matched cohorts of untreated children [118]. In addition, data from the Pfizer International Growth Database (KIGS) indicate that GH therapy in children may be associated with an increased incidence of type 2 diabetes mellitus. Diabetes mellitus is not an absolute contraindication to GHRT. However, if the patient has diabetes and GH therapy is started, glycemic control may worsen before it becomes better because of the positive effect on body composition [14]. Likewise, adults predisposed to diabetes (e.g., positive family history, personal history of gestational diabetes, metabolic syndrome) may experience a worsening of blood glucose control [89]. This suggests the importance of enhancing surveillance of individuals at risk for developing diabetes mellitus after the start of GHD. Finally, it is advisable to start GHRT with lower doses in these categories of patients. ### 7.5.3.4 Adrenal and Thyroid Function 7.3 119 120 121 122 Patients who received brain radiotherapy are chiefly at risk, as pituitary insufficiency may occur several years after the insult and GHRT might unmask central hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency during long-term follow-up. ### 7.5.3.5 Other Possible Side Effects Adverse events reported in adults on GHRT include arthralgia, fluid retention (peripheral edema), paresthesias (especially carpal tunnel syndrome), and reduced concentration [123]. These side effects are dose-dependent and are generally transient. Starting treatment with low doses of GH, gradually titrated upwards, reduces the incidence of these side effects. Benign intracranial hypertension (pseudotu mor cerebri) has been reported as a side effect of GHRT in children [124]. Lower doses of rhGH are recommended in obese patients because they are more susceptible to GHRT side effects. ## PDF page 212 | printed page 196 ### 7 ### 7.5.4 Are There Contraindications ### for Continuing GHRT? Before reinstating GHRT during transition and adulthood, it may be important to con sider the contraindications to GHRT that might exist or have developed since stopping GH therapy. The first and most important would be the development of an active malig nancy. This should be obvious by the history, but the clinician should be aware of this pos sibility. Some patients may have had a central nervous system tumor that was irradiated in childhood. This should be re-examined by an appropriate MRI image of the brain. The tumor may have recurred, or more likely, a new tumor may have developed because of irradiation to the area. Developing a second central nervous system tumor is a known risk after cranial irradiation. Another contraindication to GHRT is the presence of active proliferative or severe no proliferative diabetic retinopathy, given the proven effects of the GH/IGF-1 axis on the retina in patients with diabetes [125]. Pregnancy is not an absolute contraindica tion to GH therapy [126]. The placenta pro duces chorionic somatomammotropin during the third trimester (or even earlier) and, there fore, GH is not necessary during the last 3 months of pregnancy [109]. A feasible treat ment for pregnant GHD patient is to give two-thirds the dose in the first trimester, onethird in the second, and none in the third tri mester.
